description: We are a team of builders, programmers, entrepreneurs, and football (soccer) lovers building Builder Trails, where abandoned rovers and spacecraft teach the builders of tomorrow. Through their stories, and the engineering and design that made crucial discoveries possible, we turn retired missions into hands-on lessons that inspire the next generation to build what comes next.
summary: Builder Trails is an interactive, browser-based scrollytelling experience that transforms NASA’s retired off-world spacecraft live systems-engineering classrooms for young minds (ages 8–14). Guided by Granpa—a veteran aerospace flight director inspired by pioneering NASA leaders—students deconstruct the Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle, Opportunity (with Spirit), and Dawn through exploded hardware views, sourced NASA designs, and component-level comparisons, directly connecting specific engineering parts to the historic discoveries they made possible. Built to be more than a passive storyteller, the platform equips students with a real intuition for engineering design and the audacity to build—all running 100% client-side with zero data collected from children.
details:
Builder Trails

"Where Abandoned Machines Teach Tomorrow’s Builders"

1. Project Overview & The Core Challenge

The 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge, "Abandoned but not Forgotten," addresses a significant pedagogical gap: while active missions dominate media headlines, humanity’s retired rovers, landers, and orbiters remain parked across the Moon, Mars, and deep space as silent monuments.

School-age enthusiasts (ages 8–14) hear only about active mission while, previously sent spacecrafts are not abandoned in vain; their mechanical lessons and operational scars are the exact blueprints that make modern and future planetary exploration possible.

Builder Trails transforms these off-world monuments into a living, browser-based systems-engineering classroom. Guided by Grandpa—a veteran aerospace flight director inspired by real-world NASA leaders—students deconstruct retired spacecraft into their mechanical components, explore the scientific discoveries unlocked by those specific subsystems, and drill quizzes on the lessons they took.

2. Our Storytelling Angle: Hardware as the Storyteller

Rather than presenting a passive chronological timeline, Builder Trails flips the camera angle from the mission timeline to the machine’s internal anatomy, showing how every part contributed to that mission.

"Every discovery across the solar system occurred because a specific engineering component operated in extreme environments."

Builder Trails deconstructs three iconic eras of exploration across a clear evolutionary line:

1. APOLLO LRV-002 (Moon, 1972)

2. OPPORTUNITY & SPIRIT (Mars, 2004)

3. DAWN (Deep Space, 2007)

At each stop, the narrative connects four distinct pillars:

1. The Deconstructed Subsystem: Technical examination of batteries, wheels, chassis, and propulsion.

2. The Groundbreaking Discovery: The exact rock, soil, or geologic feature made accessible by that component.

3. The Engineering Trade-Off and The Person Behind it: Why the hardware was designed with specific constraints (e.g., single use vs. rechargeable power).

4. Grandpa's Field Wisdom: Practical design heuristics handed down to the next generation of builders.

3. The Three Explored Machines & Technical Grounding

1. Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle 002 (LRV-002) — The Moon (Descartes Highlands)

Subsystem Deconstruction:

1. Electrical Power Subsystem (EPS): Two 36-volt DC non-rechargeable silver-zinc (Ag-Zn) batteries manufactured by Eagle-Picher Industries, Inc., rated at 121 Ah each (total system: 242 Ah, 8.7 kWh). Connected in parallel to dual buses for full redundancy; either battery could independently carry the entire electrical load.

2. Mobility & Wheels: Delco/GM 81.8 cm diameter tires woven from zinc-coated high-carbon steel piano wire, fitted with titanium chevron cleats covering 50% of the contact surface to float over loose regolith. Driven by four in-hub 0.25 hp DC brush motors sealed with nitrogen at 7.5 psia to prevent arcing in vacuum.

3. Fender & Dust Vulnerability: Fiberglass fenders with sliding extension flaps. When John Young’s hammer broke the right-rear fender flap at Station 4 (Stone Mountain), high "rooster tails" of electrostatic dust coated the crew and the quartz radiator mirrors, pushing battery temperatures toward their 52°C–60°C (125°F–140°F) operating threshold.

The Breakthrough Discovery:

Expanding human exploration beyond the walking safety radius enabled the Apollo 16 crew to traverse 26.7 km across the Cayley Plains and sample North Ray Crater, recovering Sample 61016 ("Big Muley")—an 11.7 kg shock-melt breccia that remains the largest lunar rock returned by Apollo.

2. Opportunity & Her Twin Spirit (MER) — Mars (Meridiani Planum & Gusev Crater)

Subsystem Deconstruction:

1. Power Evolution: Shifting from short-duration single-use chemistry to an autonomous hybrid: 1.3 m² of multi-junction GaAs/Ge triple-junction solar panels generating up to 900 Wh/sol, backed by two rechargeable 8-cell Lithium-ion (Li-ion) battery packs (16 Ah total capacity at 28–32 V).

2. Dust Storm Survival: Telemetry tracking atmospheric optical depth (tau). When Martian dust storms drove optical depth above tau ~ 4.0–5.0, daily solar power dropped to critical survival limits (under 128 Wh/sol), requiring deep-sleep power cycles and Radioisotope Heater Units (RHUs) containing Plutonium-238 to keep internal warm electronics boxes alive.

The Breakthrough Discovery:

Microscopic imaging and Alpha Particle X-ray Spectrometry (APXS) identified hematite-rich concretions ("blueberries") and gypsum veins at Endeavour Crater, providing evidence of past, neutral-pH liquid water on Mars.

3. Dawn Spacecraft — The Asteroid Belt (Vesta & Ceres)

Subsystem Deconstruction:

1. Propulsion Evolution: Eliminating ground-contact wheels in favor of deep-space orbital transfers. Three NSTAR electrostatic xenon ion thrusters powered by supercritical xenon (425 kg propellant load), outputting continuous throttleable thrust between 19 mN and 91 mN with an ultra-efficient specific impulse (Isp) of 3,100 seconds (a 10x efficiency gain over chemical propulsion).

2. Power in Deep Space: Two 19.7 m tip-to-tip triple-junction solar wings generating 10.3 kW at 1.0 AU, tapering to 1.3 kW at Ceres (3.0 AU).

The Breakthrough Discovery:

Proving that dwarf planet Ceres is a water-rich world featuring bright sodium carbonate salt deposits (Cerealia Facula in Occator Crater) that originate from a deep subsurface briny reservoir.

4. Generational Mentorship: Meet Grandpa

To bridge complex aerospace data and middle-school learners, we introduced Grandpa—a veteran aerospace flight director inspired by real-world NASA engineers.

5. Technical Architecture, Accessibility & Safety

Modern Web Standards: Built with modern web technologies (responsive WebGL 3D transforms, lightweight interactive charts, and accessible typography) running smoothly in desktop, tablet, and school Chromebook browsers without requiring downloads or software installs.

Others InformationChild Safety by Design (COPPA/GDPR-K Aligned):

Builder Trails collects zero personal information, requires no account creation, stores no tracking cookies, and runs 100% client-side. Blueprint configurations are managed strictly in local browser memory.
